newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Azeri president in talks with Russia oil companies.
newsitem.headline: Azeri president in talks with Russia oil companies.

text.p: Azeri President Haydar Aliyev, who is keen to develop oil reserves in his country's sector of the Caspian, said on Friday he had held talks with a number of Russian oil companies during his official visit to Moscow.
He also said he was confident a key agreement between oil firms in Russia, Azerbaijan and Chechnya on exporting Azeri oil to world markets would be signed in the next few days.
"Today I spoke to representatives of (oil companies) YUKOS and SIDANKO and a number of other oil companies, and further talks will take place," he told a news conference.
Aliyev gave no further details of the talks, but was speaking in the context of Russian and other foreign oil firms developing Azerbaijan's massive offshore oil reserves.
YUKOS is Russia's second largest oil company by production and SIDANKO its fifth biggest.
Aliyev also signed two oil exploration and production deals during his visit to Moscow.
LUKoil, Russia's largest oil company, signed a $2-billion deal with Azerbaijan's state oil company SOCAR on Thursday to develop the Yalama oilfield.
LUKoil will get a 60 percent stake in the deal and SOCAR 40 percent. The field is estimated to contain around 50 million tonnes of oil.
SOCAR signed on Friday a $1-billion preliminary agreement with LUKoil and Russia's state oil company Rosneft to develop the Kyapaz oilfield.
SOCAR would get a 50 percent stake in the project, LUKoil 30 percent and Rosneft 20 percent. Kyapaz's estimated reserves are pegged at over 50 million tonnes.
Azerbaijan has signed deals worth around $20 billion with foreign oil firms hungry to tap some of the world's richest reserves.
The biggest single deal is the Azerbaijan International Operating Company (AIOC) -- an $8-billion consortium led by the British Petroleum -Statoil alliance.

The consortium plans to start output from its Caspian fields in August and is anxious to see a deal struck between Russian, Chechen and Azeri parties allowing it to transport its "early" oil from Baku to Novorossiisk on the Black Sea.
Aliyev said he expected a final commercial deal between the three sides to be signed soon.

"It was decided that three companies -- Transneft, the Azeri state oil company and the Chechen oil company would sign a commercial agreement on using the pipeline," he said. "This will be signed today, tomorrow, or the day after tomorrow."
Transneft is Russia's state-owned oil pipeline monopoly.
Signing the agreement by companies and not states appears to represent a workable compromise to avoid the thorny issue of sovereignty blocking the agreement further.
A deal has been held up for months, partly over wrangling between Russia and its independence-minded region of Chechnya.
